paragraphs: The Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. It is a city of about 600,000 people in northwestern Poland. It is a city that I would probably never have visited or known in my life if I had not studied abroad, and I studied there for about two months and had a valuable experience that I will never forget.

The Medical University of Gdansk is divided into the Polish Division (hereafter PD) and the English Division (hereafter ED). PD is a course in which Poles take the entrance examination in Polish and study medicine in Polish, and ED is a course in which English-speaking Poles who are returnees and foreigners take the entrance examination in English and study medicine in English. I took part in the clerkships of ED and was able to do my clerkships in English. This was one of the main reasons I chose to study at the Medical University of Gdansk. Also, although it is not limited to Poland, transplantation is thriving in Europe and America, so I applied to this university hoping I could see transplant surgery.

For the study abroad, I joined an ED clerkship group of about 20 people, in a form like taking part in the first polyclinic clerkship in Japan. The clerkship was structured so that we first received a one- to two-hour lecture first thing in the morning and then split into small groups of about five to do the clerkship. On the last day of the clerkship there was a simple written examination; although given the structure of the study abroad it was not necessary to pass, I thought it was a good opportunity to check how well I remembered in English what I had learned in that department, so I prepared to some extent and took the test. I did clerkships for one week in urology, two weeks in orthopedics, one week in pediatric surgery, two weeks in transplant surgery, and two weeks in gastrointestinal, breast and endocrine surgery. This too differs from other universities: because we join according to the schedule of the students' clerkship groups, I could do clerkships in many departments. The departments that left an especially strong impression were urology, orthopedics and transplant surgery.

In urology I observed robotic surgery for prostate cancer, and the robot used was not the one commonly seen at Nagoya University but an even smaller one. According to the surgeon, there are instruments that cannot be mounted compared with conventional ones, so it has pros and cons, but being able to perform robotic surgery in an ordinary small operating room was novel to me. I was also allowed to grasp and cut resected tissue with that machine. In Japan I had touched training robots but had never been allowed to operate one during surgery, so it was my first time and I was a little nervous, but it was a fantastic experience. Also, since many doctors and nurses can basically speak English, some doctors considerately held almost all conversation during surgery in English for our sake, which I was very grateful for.

In orthopedics I could see in the outpatient clinic patients who had evacuated from Ukraine because of the war. This is not limited to orthopedics: because of the war many Ukrainians have evacuated to Poland, and seeing Ukrainians did not seem unusual since the war began. However, Gdansk is far from the border with Ukraine, and I did not see any patients who seemed to have been injured in the war. That a war that feels like a fire on the other side of the river in Japan is happening right under one's nose was unthinkable in Japan. However, I would like to say that the atmosphere in the city was bright enough not to make you feel that a war was occurring in the neighboring country, so people were not living in a tense atmosphere all the time.

In transplant surgery I was actually able to take part in transplant operations. Unlike in Japan, transplantation of most organs is not between living donors, so, so as not to waste precious opportunities for observation, the transplant surgery department used a system in which recruitment was announced on its web page and several volunteers could take part on a first-come, first-served basis. I took part in a lung transplant operation, and I was surprised that lung transplants, of which only about 250 had been performed in all of Japan cumulatively up to 2019, are performed once or twice a week there, more when busy, and that students are given opportunities to take part in various transplant operations such as kidney and liver transplants as well as lung transplants.

In Gdansk, Professor Michal Wozniak looked after us. The professor has friendly ties with Nagoya University and has visited Japan many times, and he told us a lot about his experiences in Japan and memories with professors at Nagoya University. The professor looked after us well, surprising us by coming to pick us up at the airport when we arrived in the middle of the night, and often inviting us to meals. Also, for our exchange with local students and to introduce the exchange study abroad program to Nagoya University, he held an event called "Nagoya Day," where green tea and matcha were served to local students and Japanese culture and the relationship between Japanese tea and longevity were introduced. On the day, over the two days, more than 300 students in total and people from the Japanese Embassy in Warsaw came, and it was a valuable opportunity to interact with local students. Also, a student named Pawel, who belongs to the professor's laboratory, helped me with the hospital clerkship and with real life. I belong to the medical school soccer club, and he too belongs to the soccer club of the Medical University of Gdansk, and through his arrangement I was able to take part in training twice a week. Playing on a pitch where Polish was flying around was completely different from playing in Japan, and it was a very valuable experience.

As I wrote earlier, the Medical University of Gdansk has the advantage that you can study in English, so many medical students from all over Europe come to study abroad, and I did clerkships with international students from various countries, including Italy and Germany, as well as Spain, France and Slovakia. The international students we became friends with were very sociable, and we went to meals together and were invited to parties on weekends. Even in the way of having fun with friends there are differences between Japan and Europe, and we noticed such differences from each other, so it was a very meaningful time and I made friends all over Europe.

For daily life, I lived in the university dormitory and commuted to the university. Some of the dormitory matrons could only speak Polish, so struggling to communicate using a translation app is also a good memory. The university was about a ten-minute walk from the dormitory, and about a 20-minute walk from the dormitory there was a large shopping mall where I could get all my daily necessities. Prices were also lower than in Japan, and I had sent detergent and shampoo in advance, but I could buy everything more cheaply than in Japan, so it was a complete waste of money. Also, because the population density of Europe overall is lower than Japan's, I had the impression that it is much more developed than a city of 600,000 people in Japan, and I had almost no trouble in daily life. What surprised me most was how widespread English education is: not only the local students but almost everyone, apart from some slightly older shop assistants at supermarkets and convenience stores, spoke more fluent English than I did. So I had almost no trouble with being unable to communicate when shopping.

On the day I first arrived in Gdansk, I was anxious about whether I could really live in an unknown world where the townscape, culture, language and everything differed from Japan, where I had lived until then, but thanks to Professor Wozniak, Pawel, the ED students I met in the clerkships and all the other international students, I had a truly meaningful two months. The beautiful scenery of the city, which took my breath away when I first saw it, had become familiar by the time we left, and when I was packing up to leave the dormitory I felt truly sad; I fell in love with this city.

It has become a clumsy piece of writing with no structure, but I want to say above all that the roughly two months of clerkships in Poland, where I could not understand the language, became irreplaceable memories that I will never forget. I deeply thank the university that gave me this opportunity, Professor 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and everyone in the International Collaboration Office, and everyone at the Medical University of Gdansk, beginning with Professor Wozniak.
